fail2ban.intro: Fail2ban runs on the server itself. It reads the security log of Cosmos and the server's SSH log, and bans an address at the firewall after repeated failed logins, scans or abuse: a banned address reaches nothing on the server, neither Cosmos nor the apps nor SSH, until the ban ends.
fail2ban.jail.abuse.watches: Strikes and bans given by SmartShield: an address SmartShield blocks inside Cosmos is then blocked on every port.
fail2ban.jail.auth.watches: Failed logins, wrong two-factor codes, wrong password at the confirmation prompt, bad invitation or reset links, API tokens that do not exist.
fail2ban.jail.counts: Banned now: {{now}}. Banned since Fail2ban started: {{total}}. Tries being counted: {{failed}}.
fail2ban.jail.probe.watches: Requests for paths only scanners ask for, such as /.env, /wp-login.php or /.git/config.
fail2ban.jail.recidive.watches: Addresses banned again and again by the other jails: they get a much longer ban.
fail2ban.jail.scan.watches: Requests for host names this server does not serve (a scan of its address) and bots refused by a URL's bot filter.
fail2ban.jail.sshd.watches: Failed logins to the server itself over SSH.
fail2ban.jails.intro: A jail watches one kind of misbehaviour. An address that reaches the number of tries within the time they are counted over is banned for the length of the ban.
fail2ban.jails.notInstalled: The jails of this fork are not installed on the server yet, so there is nothing to set here. What is shown is what the installer would set up.
fail2ban.jails.title: Jails and their thresholds

mgmt.config.email.address.help: The mailbox Cosmos sends from, for example cosmos@example.com. The server settings are found from it.

mgmt.config.email.advice.appPassword: This provider wants an app password instead of the normal password. Create one in the account's security settings and enter it as the password.
mgmt.config.email.advice.appPassword.url: This provider wants an app password instead of the normal password. Create one at {{url}} and enter it as the password.
mgmt.config.email.advice.auth: Signing in failed. Check the user name and the password.
mgmt.config.email.advice.authDisabled: Sign-in with a password is switched off for this mailbox ("Authenticated SMTP" at Microsoft 365). An administrator of the organisation has to switch it on for the mailbox; otherwise use another mail service.
mgmt.config.email.advice.authNeedsTls: The password is only sent over an encrypted connection. Choose 465 or 587 with encryption under custom settings.
mgmt.config.email.advice.authNoMethod: This server takes no password here, only ways of signing in that Cosmos cannot use. Use an app password if the provider offers one, or another mail service.
mgmt.config.email.advice.certExpired: The certificate of the mail server is out of date; whoever runs it has to renew it. Also check the clock of this server.
mgmt.config.email.advice.certName: The certificate was issued for another name than the one entered. Use the server name the provider documents; an alias of it does not do.
mgmt.config.email.advice.certUntrusted: The certificate of the mail server cannot be verified. If it is your own server with a self-signed certificate, switch on "Accept a certificate that cannot be verified" under custom settings. With a provider on the internet, stop here: something may be in between.
mgmt.config.email.advice.connect: The connection ended before the mail server greeted. Check the server name and the port.
mgmt.config.email.advice.hostNotFound: The server name does not exist. Check its spelling under custom settings.
mgmt.config.email.advice.needsSignIn: The server only takes mail from senders who sign in. Enter the user name and the password.
mgmt.config.email.advice.needsTls: The server wants encryption before it takes mail. Choose "587 · encrypted after connecting (STARTTLS)".
mgmt.config.email.advice.noStartTLS: The server offers no encryption on this port. Try port 465, encrypted from the start. Only for a mail server on your own network: "Other", not encrypted.
mgmt.config.email.advice.notTls: This port does not start encrypted. Choose "587 · encrypted after connecting (STARTTLS)".
mgmt.config.email.advice.recipient: The server refused the recipient. Check the address the test is sent to.
mgmt.config.email.advice.refused: The server is there, but nothing listens on port {{port}}. Try {{other}} under custom settings.
mgmt.config.email.advice.rejected: The mail server refused the user name or the password. Check both: the user name is usually the whole email address, and the password must be typed exactly.
mgmt.config.email.advice.rejectedApp: {{name}} refused the sign-in. It does not take the normal password of the account: create an app password in the account's security settings and enter that. Also check the user name: it is the whole email address.
mgmt.config.email.advice.rejectedApp.url: {{name}} refused the sign-in. It does not take the normal password of the account: create an app password at {{url}} and enter that. Also check the user name: it is the whole email address.
mgmt.config.email.advice.send: The server refused the message itself. Its reason is in the detail.
mgmt.config.email.advice.sender: The server refused the sender address. It usually has to be the address of the mailbox you sign in with, or one verified at the mail service.
mgmt.config.email.advice.timeout: Nothing answered on port {{port}}. Your internet provider or hosting company may block it, or the server uses the other port: try {{other}} under custom settings.
mgmt.config.email.advice.timeout25: Nothing answered on port 25. Most internet providers block it: choose 587 or 465 under custom settings.
mgmt.config.email.advice.tls: The encryption could not be set up. Try the other port ({{other}}).
mgmt.config.email.advice.tlsExpected: Port 465 expects encryption from the first moment. Choose "465 · encrypted from the start (TLS)".
mgmt.config.email.advice.tryLater: The mail server asks to try again later. Wait a few minutes; if it stays like this, the provider may be limiting the account.
mgmt.config.email.advice.unknown: Check the server name, the port and the sign-in under custom settings.
mgmt.config.email.advice.unreachable: This server has no way to reach the mail server. Check the server name and this server's network.
mgmt.config.email.check.certExpired: It answered on port {{port}} just now, but its certificate is out of date.
mgmt.config.email.check.certName: It answered on port {{port}} just now, but its certificate was issued for another name.
mgmt.config.email.check.certUntrusted: It answered on port {{port}} just now, but its certificate cannot be verified (self-signed, or from an authority this server does not know).
mgmt.config.email.check.local: This name points to this server itself or to an address that is never contacted automatically. If that is what you want, enter it under custom settings.
mgmt.config.email.check.noAnswer: It did not answer on port {{port}} from this server just now: the port may be blocked on the way, or this server has no connection to the internet.
mgmt.config.email.check.noPassword: It answered on port {{port}} just now, but offers no sign-in with a password.
mgmt.config.email.check.noStartTLS: It answered on port {{port}}, but offers no encryption there.
mgmt.config.email.check.notChecked: Not checked (an unusual port, or time ran out).
mgmt.config.email.check.notSmtp: Something answered on port {{port}} that is not a mail server.
mgmt.config.email.check.ok: It answered on port {{port}} just now, with a certificate that was verified.
mgmt.config.email.check.tlsFailed: It answered on port {{port}}, but the encryption could not be set up.
mgmt.config.email.conn.25.desc: The port mail servers use among themselves. Most internet providers block it; a mail server on your own network may only listen here.
mgmt.config.email.conn.465.desc: Encrypted from the first moment. Offered by nearly every provider; try it first.
mgmt.config.email.conn.587.desc: Starts plain and is encrypted before anything is sent. The choice when 465 is not offered (Microsoft 365, iCloud).
mgmt.config.email.conn.label: Port and encryption
mgmt.config.email.conn.other.desc: Another port, such as 2525, or a server without encryption.

mgmt.config.email.detect.looking: Looking for the mail servers of {{domain}}: a few seconds…

mgmt.config.email.enc.on465: Port 465 is always encrypted from the start (TLS).
mgmt.config.email.enc.onDesc: The connection is encrypted before the password or a mail is sent. The server must offer STARTTLS.

mgmt.urls.guide.hostSeen: The app receives its requests under the name {{host}}. Some apps only answer to names they know (Radarr and Sonarr say "Invalid Hostname", others speak of allowed or trusted hosts): if the app refuses, add {{host}} in the app's own settings.
mgmt.urls.guide.error.hostRequired: Enter the address, for example radarr.local
mgmt.urls.guide.error.hostDot: Write the whole name with a dot, such as radarr.local or films.example.org
mgmt.urls.guide.error.hostProtocol: Leave out http:// and https://: only the name
mgmt.urls.guide.error.nameRequired: Give the URL a name, for example the app's
mgmt.urls.guide.why.mode: it serves a folder or redirects
mgmt.urls.guide.why.socket: it forwards a port that is not a web address
mgmt.urls.guide.why.noHost: it has no address of its own
mgmt.urls.guide.why.access: its access settings do not match one of the three choices
mgmt.urls.guide.summaryNoShield: Saved as "{{name}}". The protection against abuse (Smart Shield) is switched off for it: see "All settings".
mgmt.urls.guide.port.usualHeld: This URL leads to port {{current}}. If the address shows "502 Bad Gateway", the port is the first thing to check.
mgmt.urls.all.why.stopped: not running, so its ports are not known: start it first
mgmt.urls.all.why.hostNetwork: uses the server's own network: it is reached at the server's address and its own port
mgmt.urls.all.why.taken: the address {{host}} or the name is already used by another URL
mgmt.urls.all.why.noAddress: no free address could be proposed
mgmt.urls.all.why.guess: declares no port; {{port}} would be a guess: use New on its card
mgmt.urls.all.why.noPort: has no port to point at (not a web app, or its port is not declared): use New on its card if it has a web page
mgmt.urls.all.title: A local address for the apps that have none
mgmt.urls.all.text: Each ticked app gets the address shown. It works on the local network only: nothing becomes reachable from the internet. Every address can be changed or deleted afterwards under URLs.
mgmt.urls.all.nothing: No app is left that an address can be proposed for.
mgmt.urls.all.hostHint: Each app receives its requests under its new name. Apps that only answer to names they know (Radarr and Sonarr say "Invalid Hostname") need that name added in their own settings.
mgmt.urls.guide.notSimple: All settings are shown, because the simple view cannot show this URL: {{reasons}}.
mgmt.urls.guide.port.unknown: The app does not declare port {{port}}. If nothing answers there, the address shows "502 Bad Gateway".
mgmt.urls.guide.port.noApp: No app named {{app}} is on this server right now, so its ports are not known.
mgmt.urls.guide.error.port: Pick the port of the app
mgmt.urls.guide.intro: Pick the address. The rest is proposed; change what does not fit.
mgmt.urls.guide.mode.label: What should the address open?
mgmt.urls.guide.mode.appHint: A container that runs here, such as Jellyfin or Radarr.
mgmt.urls.guide.mode.proxyHint: A web page elsewhere on your network, such as the router or a NAS.
mgmt.urls.guide.app.label: App
mgmt.urls.guide.app.placeholder: Pick the app the address opens
mgmt.urls.guide.address.label: Address
mgmt.urls.guide.address.help: What people type to open it, without http://. For example radarr.local, or films.example.org with a domain of yours.
mgmt.urls.guide.port.labelOf: Port of {{app}} the address leads to
mgmt.urls.guide.port.label: Port of the app
mgmt.urls.guide.scheme.label: The app speaks
mgmt.urls.guide.scheme.http: What nearly every app speaks. It is only how Cosmos talks to the app inside the server.
mgmt.urls.guide.scheme.https: For a port that is the app's own HTTPS port (443, 8443…). The app's self-made certificate is accepted.
mgmt.urls.guide.proxy.label: Where it leads
mgmt.urls.guide.proxy.help: The address of the other page, with http:// or https:// and its port. For example http://192.168.1.1:8080.
mgmt.urls.guide.proxy.insecure: Accept its certificate without checking it
mgmt.urls.guide.proxy.insecureHelp: Needed for devices with a self-made certificate: most routers, NAS and printers.
mgmt.urls.guide.access.label: Who may open it
mgmt.urls.guide.access.anyoneHint: Cosmos asks nothing: the app's own sign-in is what protects it. Fine for apps with their own accounts.
mgmt.urls.guide.access.usersHint: Cosmos asks for its sign-in first. For apps without a sign-in of their own.
mgmt.urls.guide.access.adminsHint: Cosmos asks for its sign-in and lets administrators through only.
mgmt.urls.guide.name.label: Name in the list of URLs
mgmt.urls.guide.summary: Saved as "{{name}}", with the protection against abuse (Smart Shield) switched on.
mgmt.urls.external.title: Also reachable from the internet through (optional):
mgmt.urls.external.forwardByHand: Automatic port forwarding is off: forward port {{port}} (HTTPS) to this server on your router by hand, or switch it on under Configuration > HTTP > Internet access.
mgmt.urls.domains.title: Domains of {{name}}
mgmt.urls.domains.text: Each ticked domain gives the app one more address, reachable from the internet: a copy of its URL {{name}}, with the same target and settings. Unticking a domain deletes that address.
mgmt.urls.domains.own: A domain that cannot be unticked is the address of the URL itself: change or delete that URL from its settings.
mgmt.reach.check.access.noHost: This URL has no address of its own, and Cosmos' own address is a local one.
mgmt.reach.check.access.localGuard: A local address: Cosmos refuses it to visitors from outside the local network.
mgmt.reach.check.access.constellation: Only the devices of your Constellation may open this URL.
mgmt.reach.check.access.whitelist: Only the addresses listed in the URL's settings may open it.
mgmt.reach.check.access.adminOnly: Open to the internet; only admins get in, after logging in.
mgmt.reach.check.access.login: Open to the internet; visitors log in to Cosmos first.
mgmt.reach.check.access.open: Open to everyone who reaches the address.
mgmt.reach.check.dns.pointsHere: The name points to this server.
mgmt.reach.check.dns.noRecord: The name does not exist in DNS. Create the record at your DNS provider, or let Cosmos manage the domain's records.
mgmt.reach.check.dns.lookupFailed: The name could not be looked up just now.
mgmt.reach.check.dns.localAnswer: Here the name resolves to a local address, probably a local DNS entry (router, Pi-hole): what the internet gets cannot be seen from here.
mgmt.reach.check.dns.publicIPUnknown: The name points to a public address, but Cosmos does not know this server's public address, so it cannot tell whether that is this server.
mgmt.reach.check.dns.pointsElsewhere: The name points to another address than this server's public one. Correct the DNS record (behind a proxy such as Cloudflare this is expected).
mgmt.reach.check.dns.badName: This address is not a name that can be looked up.
mgmt.reach.check.dns.tooMany: Not checked: too many addresses at once.
mgmt.reach.check.dns.ipNotPublic: The address is not a public one.
mgmt.reach.check.dns.ipPublicIPUnknown: The address is a public one, but Cosmos does not know this server's public address, so it cannot tell whether it is this server.
mgmt.reach.check.dns.ipElsewhere: The address is not this server's public address.
mgmt.reach.check.dns.ipIsServer: The address is this server's public address.
mgmt.reach.check.forward.upnp: The router forwards port {{external}} to Cosmos' port {{port}} (automatic port forwarding).
mgmt.reach.check.forward.byHand: Cosmos cannot tell whether your router forwards port {{port}} to this server. Forward it on the router, or switch on automatic forwarding.
mgmt.reach.check.forward.ownPort: This URL uses port {{port}} of its own: Cosmos cannot tell whether the router forwards it.
mgmt.reach.check.forward.ipv6Firewall: Reached over IPv6: nothing to forward, but the router's IPv6 firewall must let port {{port}} in, and Cosmos cannot see it.
mgmt.reach.check.forward.routerNotPublic: The router's own internet address is not a public one (provider NAT): nothing behind it can be reached from the internet.
mgmt.reach.check.cert.selfSigned: The certificate is not one browsers trust: visitors get a warning. Use Let's Encrypt for the domain.
mgmt.reach.check.cert.wrongName: The certificate does not cover this name: visitors get a warning.
mgmt.reach.check.cert.expired: The certificate has expired: visitors get a warning.
mgmt.reach.check.cert.none: No certificate is ready for this name yet.
mgmt.reach.check.cert.ipAddress: Browsers do not trust a certificate for an IP address: give the app a name.
mgmt.reach.check.cert.plainHTTP: Served over plain HTTP: nothing is encrypted.
mgmt.reach.tip.verified: Checked from the server: the name points here, the router forwards the port and the certificate is valid. Nobody tested it from outside. Click to open {{url}}.
mgmt.reach.tip.unverified: Open to the internet at {{host}}, but not everything could be checked: {{reason}} Click to open it.
mgmt.reach.tip.hostNetwork: No internet address through Cosmos. It uses the server's own network, so its ports are the server's: reachable from the local network, from the internet only if your router forwards them. Cosmos cannot tell.
mgmt.reach.tip.ports: No internet address through Cosmos. Published on the server: port {{ports}}. Reachable from the local network; from the internet only if your router forwards it, which Cosmos cannot tell.
mgmt.reach.tip.limited: Its URL may be opened only from the addresses listed in its settings, or from the Constellation.
mgmt.reach.tip.local: Only local addresses: not reachable from the internet.
mgmt.reach.tip.none: No URL and no published port: not reachable from outside.
mgmt.reach.tooSoon: Checked moments ago: try again in a few seconds.
mgmt.reach.lookupFailed: The public address could not be looked up.
mgmt.reach.port.server: Port {{port}} is published for this server only ({{ip}}): not reachable from other devices.
mgmt.reach.port.address: Port {{port}} is published on the address {{ip}} only. From the internet only if your router forwards it; Cosmos cannot tell.
mgmt.reach.port.all: Port {{port}} ({{type}}) is published on the server: reachable from the local network; from the internet only if your router forwards it, which Cosmos cannot tell.
mgmt.reach.port.host: Uses the server's own network: every port it listens on is a port of the server. From the internet only if your router forwards it.
mgmt.reach.publicIPKnown: Cosmos knows this server's public address ({{source}}).
mgmt.reach.publicIPUnknown: Cosmos does not know this server's public address: it learns it from automatic port forwarding or from DynDNS.
mgmt.reach.checkedAt: Checked {{time}} from the server. Nothing is tested from outside your network: only a device outside it (a phone on mobile data) can confirm.
mgmt.reach.askPublicIPTip: Asks api.ipify.org (then icanhazip.com, checkip.amazonaws.com: the services DynDNS uses) which address this server shows up with. Only on this click; the answer is kept for six hours.
mgmt.reach.title: Internet
mgmt.router.externalPortNote: From the internet, addresses under your domains are reached on port {{port}}: https://{{example}}
mgmt.router.meaning: A port opened this way reaches the app directly from the internet: without Cosmos' login, without SmartShield, without the HTTPS Cosmos provides, and Fail2ban does not see the app's own sign-ins. The app's own protection is all there is.
mgmt.router.dialog.externalInvalid: Enter a port between 1 and 65535, or leave it empty
mgmt.router.dialog.externalReserved: Cosmos never asks the router for port {{port}} (Internet access, reserved ports)
mgmt.router.dialog.title: Open port {{port}} ({{protocol}}) of {{name}} on the router?
mgmt.router.dialog.webRoute: This port is the app's web interface, and the app already has an address through Cosmos: {{address}}. That address is the safer way and needs no extra port. Open the port only if something has to reach the app directly.
mgmt.router.dialog.webGuess: Port {{port}} looks like a web interface. For a web page, give the app a URL instead ("New" under URLs): it goes through Cosmos' one HTTPS port, with login and SmartShield, and needs no extra port.
mgmt.router.dialog.purpose: Opening a port is for what is not a web page or has to be reached directly: peer ports, game servers, media clients. For a web interface the app's URL through Cosmos is the safer way.
mgmt.router.dialog.schemeFromPort: Proposed from the port number: change it if it is wrong.
mgmt.router.dialog.schemeHelp: A web page gets a link; anything else is shown as an address to copy.
mgmt.router.dialog.externalHelp: Empty: {{port}}, the port the container publishes. If the router has it taken, Cosmos uses the next free port above it and says so; it never takes a port from another device.
mgmt.router.dialog.limits: Cosmos asks the router over UPnP. It cannot see forwards entered in the router's own pages: such a port may be refused, or accepted without effect. Only IPv4 is forwarded; over IPv6 nothing is opened.
mgmt.router.links.group: Internet, by port (opened on the router)
mgmt.router.install.title: Open a port on the router as well? (optional)
mgmt.router.install.text: The app publishes these ports on the server. Each can also be opened on your router (UPnP), so it is reached from the internet directly. Nothing is opened unless you tick it. A web interface needs none: the app's URL goes through Cosmos.
mgmt.router.install.pending: What is ticked is opened on the router once the app is created, and is then reachable from the internet directly, without Cosmos' login.
mgmt.router.install.opened: Port {{port}} of {{name}}: the router forwards port {{external}}.
mgmt.router.overview.title: Ports open on the router
mgmt.router.overview.none: Cosmos holds no port open on the router.
mgmt.router.overview.forwarded: {{protocol}} port {{external}} on the router goes to port {{internal}} here
mgmt.router.overview.paused: Cosmos does not try this one again by itself: press "Check now". The other ports are renewed as usual.
mgmt.router.overview.holder: Port {{port}} is used by {{holder}}: another device on your network. Cosmos does not take it.
mgmt.router.overview.suggest: Port {{port}} looks free on the router. Cosmos does not move its own port by itself: another external port changes every external address of your apps, and behind Cloudflare only 443, 2053, 2083, 2087, 2096 and 8443 work.
mgmt.router.overview.suggestTaken: Port {{port}} is in the form: press Save to use it.
mgmt.router.foreign.title: Other ports open on the router (not Cosmos')
mgmt.router.foreign.notAsked: Cosmos has not talked to the router: it does so when a port is to be opened, or on "Check now" while something is switched on.
mgmt.router.foreign.notListed: This router does not let its port mappings be listed.
mgmt.router.foreign.none: The router lists no other port mapping.
mgmt.router.foreign.rowHere: {{protocol}} port {{external}} goes to port {{internal}} of this server, opened by another program here
mgmt.router.foreign.row: {{protocol}} port {{external}} goes to {{client}}, port {{internal}}: another device on your network
mgmt.router.foreign.truncated: The list is longer than what Cosmos reads (128 entries).
mgmt.router.foreign.limits: This is what the router shows over UPnP. Forwards entered in the router's own pages are often not in it, and Cosmos cannot see them: asked for such a port, a router may refuse, or accept without any effect. Cosmos never changes or removes a mapping it did not create. Only IPv4 is forwarded this way.
mgmt.router.overview.closeOwnTitle: Close Cosmos' {{name}} port on the router?
mgmt.router.overview.closeOwnHttp: The router stops forwarding the HTTP port and "Also forward the HTTP port" is switched off in the settings.
mgmt.router.overview.closeOwnHttps: Automatic port forwarding for Cosmos is switched off in the settings: Cosmos and every app address under your domains can no longer be reached from the internet, unless the router forwards the port by other means. Ports of apps stay as they are.
mgmt.reach.tip.forwarded: No internet address through Cosmos, but your router forwards port {{ports}} to this app (opened by Cosmos over UPnP). It reaches the app directly, without Cosmos' login. Nobody tested it from outside.
mgmt.config.internet.reserved.label: External ports Cosmos never asks the router for
mgmt.config.internet.reserved.help: Empty: the list shown (web and mail). A port forwarded in the router's own pages to another device is often invisible to Cosmos: list such ports here, and Cosmos never asks for them, neither for itself nor for an app. "none" for no port.
mgmt.config.internet.reserved.validation: Enter port numbers separated by commas, "none", or leave it empty for the usual list

mgmt.router.note.movedHolder: {{external}} on the router, because {{wanted}} is used by {{holder}}.
mgmt.router.note.movedReserved: {{external}} on the router, because Cosmos never asks a router for port {{wanted}}.
mgmt.router.state.active: The router forwards port {{external}} to port {{internal}} of this server (opened by Cosmos over UPnP). It reaches the app directly, without Cosmos' login. Not tested from outside.
mgmt.router.state.stopped: Closed on the router while the container is stopped; opened again when it runs.
mgmt.router.state.gone: The container is gone: the port is closed on the router and the choice is forgotten after a few minutes.
mgmt.router.state.notPublished: The container no longer publishes this port: it is closed on the router and the choice is forgotten after a few minutes.
mgmt.router.state.localOnly: The port is published for this server only (127.0.0.1): there is nothing a router could forward to.
mgmt.router.state.otherAddress: The port is published on another address than the one the router reaches this server on: not forwarded.
mgmt.router.state.cosmosPort: This is one of Cosmos' own ports: it is opened under Internet access, never as an app's.
mgmt.router.state.dockerUnavailable: Docker did not answer: Cosmos cannot tell whether the port is still published.
mgmt.router.state.router: The router did not answer. Cosmos does not try again by itself: press "Check now" under Internet access.
mgmt.router.state.conflict: Not opened: the port and the ones tried after it are in use on the router. Cosmos does not try again by itself: press "Check now" under Internet access, or choose another external port.
mgmt.router.state.conflictHolder: Not opened: port {{wanted}} is used by {{holder}}, and the ones tried after it are taken too. Cosmos does not try again by itself: press "Check now" under Internet access, or choose another external port.
mgmt.router.state.reserved: Not opened: port {{wanted}} is on the list of ports Cosmos never asks a router for.
mgmt.router.state.refused: The router refused: {{error}} Cosmos does not try again by itself: press "Check now" under Internet access.
mgmt.router.state.failed: The router did not open the port. Cosmos does not try again by itself: press "Check now" under Internet access.

mgmt.cron.error.count: A schedule has 6 parts separated by spaces (second, minute, hour, day of the month, month, day of the week). This one has {{count}}.
mgmt.cron.error.descriptor: "{{text}}" is not known. The words that work are @hourly, @daily, @weekly, @monthly, @yearly and @every followed by a duration such as 1h30m.
mgmt.cron.error.empty: Enter a schedule, or pick one below.
mgmt.cron.error.every: After @every comes a duration such as 30s, 15m or 1h30m.
mgmt.cron.error.field: {{field}}: "{{text}}" is not understood. Use a number, *, a list (1,15), a range (1-5) or a step (*/2).
mgmt.cron.error.five: This has 5 parts; Cosmos needs 6, the first one being the seconds. Put "0 " in front of it.
mgmt.cron.error.never: This schedule never comes up (such a date does not exist).
mgmt.cron.error.order: {{field}}: in "{{text}}" the range starts after it ends.
mgmt.cron.error.range: {{field}} goes from {{min}} to {{max}}: "{{text}}" does not fit.
mgmt.cron.error.step: {{field}}: in "{{text}}" the number after "/" must be 1 or more.
mgmt.cron.error.weekday: {{field}} goes from 0 (Sunday) to 6 (Saturday), or SUN to SAT: "{{text}}" does not fit.
mgmt.cron.error.zone: The time zone "{{zone}}" is not known. Write it like Europe/Paris.
mgmt.cron.error.zoneAlone: After the time zone comes a space and then the schedule.

mgmt.config.snapshots.destinationHelp: On a disk formatted for Linux (ext4, XFS, Btrfs…), in a place the apps cannot reach, and preferably not on the disk the folders themselves are on. It is created if it does not exist.
mgmt.config.snapshots.destinationLabel: Destination: the folder the snapshots are stored in
mgmt.config.snapshots.destinationRequire: Choose the folder the snapshots are stored in
mgmt.config.snapshots.enableLabel: Make snapshots of the folders below on a schedule
mgmt.config.snapshots.excludesHelp: For example *.tmp, cache or transcodes. A pattern without "/" applies to the name of a file or folder at any depth; one with "/" applies to the path below each folder backed up, for example downloads/incomplete. A folder that is left out is skipped with all it holds. "*" and "?" stay within one name; "**" is not supported.
mgmt.config.snapshots.excludesLabel: Files and folders to leave out (one pattern per line)
mgmt.config.snapshots.excludesValidation: At most 100 patterns, each at most 200 characters, one per line. A pattern must not start with "/", go up with "..", or contain "**".
mgmt.config.snapshots.frequency: How often a snapshot is made
mgmt.config.snapshots.info: Cosmos keeps dated copies (snapshots) of the folders below in the destination: one folder per date, which any file manager can open. mgmt.config.http.allowInsecureLocalAcces: Allow insecure access via local IP

When HTTPS is used along side a domain, depending on your networking configuration, it is possible that your server is not receiving direct local connections.
This option allows you to also access your Cosmos admin using your local IP address, like ip:port.
You can already create ip:port URLs for your apps, but this will make them HTTP-only.

This option is not recommended as it exposes your server to security risks on your local network.
Your local network is safer than the internet, but not safe, as devices like IoTs, smart-TVs, smartphones or even your router can be compromised.
If you want to have a secure offline / local-only access to a server that uses a domain name and HTTPS, use Constellation instead.

mgmt.seaweedfs.createDesc: Creates an S3-compatible SeaweedFS cluster: three pinned masters, one volume server on every tagged node, and a filer + S3 gateway behind the load balancer. A managed database is provisioned automatically for the filer metadata.

mgmt.seaweedfs.replication.001: one extra copy on another node (survives losing one node)

mgmt.seaweedfs.jobs.title: Maintenance jobs
mgmt.seaweedfs.jobs.desc: Scheduled cluster maintenance. Schedules are 6-field crontabs (seconds first) and run from the constellation leader.
mgmt.seaweedfs.jobs.ecDesc: By default every volume is kept as two full copies on different nodes (replication 001), so a lost node is recoverable. Erasure coding (EC) is a cost saver on top of that: cold, full volumes are re-encoded as 10 data + 4 parity shards spread across nodes, keeping the data recoverable at ~1.4x its size instead of 2x. Converting a volume temporarily needs about twice its size free, which is why it is off by default and skipped below a minimum free-disk percentage.
mgmt.seaweedfs.jobs.repackDesc: Runs automatically whenever erasure coding is on: deleted objects inside an erasure-coded volume cannot be vacuumed in place, so repacking is the only way that space is ever reclaimed.

trust.title: Understanding Self-Signed Certificates
trust.intro.first: HTTPS uses certificates to encrypt data between your browser and the sites you visit. In your home server, you have the choices between a public certificate from a Certificate Authority (CA) which is trusted by all browsers, or a self-signed certificate which is not trusted by default. A public certificate requires a full domain name, that is why Cosmos fallsback to a self-signed certificate when an IP, or a .local domain is used. In order to ensure maximum security, you can setup Cosmos as a CA, in case you need to use a self-signed certificate. This will tell your browser to trust the certificates issued by Cosmos.

security.kind.access.denied.label: Permission refused
security.kind.access.denied.todo: Usually a user opening a page they may not use. If it repeats, check that user's role.
security.kind.access.denied.what: A signed-in user or an API token asked for something it has no permission for.
security.kind.access.grant.denied.label: Refused to hand out a permission
security.kind.access.grant.denied.todo: This does not happen by accident: check who it was and what their role allows.
security.kind.access.grant.denied.what: Someone who may manage users or tokens tried to give a permission they do not hold themselves.
security.kind.access.ip.denied.label: Address not allowed
security.kind.access.ip.denied.todo: Nothing, if it was a stranger. If it was you, add your address to the URL's allowed addresses.
security.kind.access.ip.denied.what: A request came from an address that is not on an allowed list (the admin address restriction or a URL's own).
security.kind.access.local.denied.label: Local-only URL asked from outside
security.kind.access.local.denied.todo: Nothing to do. To reach it from outside, change the URL's settings.
security.kind.access.local.denied.what: A URL that is served on the local network only was asked for from the internet.
security.kind.access.origin.denied.label: Not through Cloudflare's proxy
security.kind.access.origin.denied.todo: Nothing to do: someone knows the server's own address and tried it, directly or through Cloudflare's network. If it is you, use the address through Cloudflare, or switch that address to "Directly". If your own visits are refused since you required the certificate, press "Stop enforcing" under Configuration > Domains > Cloudflare.
security.kind.access.origin.denied.what: An address that is served through Cloudflare's proxy was asked for another way: directly, from an address that is neither Cloudflare's nor on your local network, or from one of Cloudflare's addresses without the certificate that shows its proxy made the request.
security.kind.auth.login.failed.label: Failed sign-in
security.kind.auth.login.failed.todo: Nothing, if it was a user mistyping. Many attempts from one internet address are password guessing: SmartShield blocks the address after 20 in an hour, and strong passwords with two-factor sign-in keep the accounts safe.
security.kind.auth.login.failed.what: Someone tried to sign in with a wrong user name or password.
security.kind.auth.mfa.failed.label: Wrong two-factor code
security.kind.auth.mfa.failed.todo: Usually a typo. If it was not the user, someone knows that account's password: change it.
security.kind.auth.mfa.failed.what: A wrong two-factor code was entered after the right password.
security.kind.auth.mfa.locked.label: Two-factor check locked
security.kind.auth.mfa.locked.todo: Whoever tried knows the account's password. Unless it was the user, change that password now.
security.kind.auth.mfa.locked.what: After too many wrong two-factor codes Cosmos closed the code check of the account for a while.
security.kind.auth.register.failed.label: Bad invitation link
security.kind.auth.register.failed.todo: If a user cannot get in, make a new link for them. Many attempts mean someone is guessing links.
security.kind.auth.register.failed.what: Someone used an invitation or password reset link that is wrong or has expired.
security.kind.auth.reset.rejected.label: Password reset for an unknown account
security.kind.auth.reset.rejected.todo: Nothing to do: nothing was sent.
security.kind.auth.reset.rejected.what: The "forgot password" form was sent with a name and email that match no account.
security.kind.auth.reset.requested.label: Password reset asked for
security.kind.auth.reset.requested.todo: Harmless if the user asked for it. If not, the link only reaches the account's own mailbox: the user can ignore it.
security.kind.auth.reset.requested.what: Someone sent the "forgot password" form with the name and email of an account: a reset link was mailed to that account's address.
security.kind.auth.session.forged.label: Forged session
security.kind.auth.session.forged.todo: Nothing to do: it was refused. Once per browser is normal after Cosmos' sign-in key was renewed; many from one address are an attempt to break in.
security.kind.auth.session.forged.what: A browser showed a session cookie that this server never issued, or that was altered.
security.kind.auth.session.rejected.todo: Harmless: the user is asked to sign in again.
security.kind.auth.session.rejected.what: A browser showed a session that is no longer valid (it expired, or the password was changed).
security.kind.auth.sudo.failed.label: Wrong password at the confirmation
security.kind.auth.sudo.failed.todo: Usually a typo. If you do not know that session, change the user's password: it signs out every session.
security.kind.auth.sudo.failed.what: A signed-in user typed a wrong password when Cosmos asked to confirm it before a change.
security.kind.recorder.dropped.label: Security events lost
security.kind.recorder.dropped.todo: If it happens again, check the free disk space and the load of the server.
security.kind.recorder.dropped.what: Cosmos could not store some security events in time because the database did not answer.
security.kind.scan.probe.label: Probe for a known weakness
security.kind.scan.probe.todo: Nothing to do: automated scanners try this on every server on the internet.
security.kind.scan.probe.what: Someone asked for a file that attack tools look for (/.env, /wp-login.php, /.git/config and the like). It does not exist here.
security.kind.shield.ban.permanent.label: Permanent ban
security.kind.shield.ban.permanent.todo: Nothing to do. Lift the ban only if the address is one of yours.
security.kind.shield.ban.permanent.what: An address that was banned again and again stays banned until you lift the ban.
security.kind.shield.ban.temporary.label: Temporary ban
security.kind.shield.ban.temporary.todo: Nothing to do. If it is one of your own devices, lift the ban in the list of addresses.
security.kind.shield.ban.temporary.what: An address that was blocked three times is banned for a longer while.
security.kind.firewall.ban.label: Banned by Fail2ban
security.kind.firewall.ban.todo: Nothing to do. If it is one of your own devices, lift the ban in the Fail2ban section of this page.
security.kind.firewall.ban.what: Fail2ban banned an address at the firewall: nothing from it reaches the server until the ban ends.
security.kind.server.update.rejected.tod: Check that the newest release on GitHub is one you published. If it is, publish it again; if it is not, change the password of the GitHub account.
security.kind.server.update.rejected.wha: A release was not installed because it could not be verified as signed by this fork. The server stays on the version it runs.
security.kind.shield.blocked.label: Request from a blocked address
security.kind.shield.blocked.todo: Nothing to do: the block is working.
security.kind.shield.blocked.what: SmartShield turned a request away because its sender is over its limits or banned.
security.kind.shield.bot.blocked.label: Bot blocked
security.kind.shield.bot.blocked.todo: Nothing to do. If an app of yours is refused, turn the bot filter off in that URL's settings.
security.kind.shield.bot.blocked.what: A URL's bot filter refused a request that did not say which browser sent it, or came from a listed bot.
security.kind.shield.geo.blocked.label: Blocked by country
security.kind.shield.geo.blocked.what: A request came from a country your settings block.
security.kind.shield.hostname.unknown.to: Background noise of the internet: nothing to do. From the local network it means a device opens Cosmos by its IP address.
security.kind.shield.hostname.unknown.wh: A request asked for a server name this server does not serve: typically a scanner trying the bare IP address.
security.kind.shield.ratelimited.label: Too many requests
security.kind.shield.ratelimited.todo: Nothing to do. If it is an app of yours, it may be stuck in a loop.
security.kind.shield.ratelimited.what: An address sent more than 500 requests a minute and was slowed down.
security.kind.shield.strike.label: Blocked for an hour
security.kind.shield.strike.todo: Nothing to do. If it is one of your own devices, lift the block in the list of addresses.
security.kind.shield.strike.what: An address went over a SmartShield limit (requests, failed sign-ins or data) and is blocked for an hour.
security.kind.token.expired.label: Expired API token
security.kind.token.expired.todo: If an app of yours stopped working, give it a new token.
security.kind.token.expired.what: A request came with an API token that has expired.
security.kind.token.invalid.label: Unknown API token
security.kind.token.invalid.todo: A script or app may still use a deleted token: give it a new one. Otherwise someone is guessing tokens.
security.kind.token.invalid.what: A request came with an API token that does not exist.
security.kind.token.ip.denied.label: API token from a wrong address
security.kind.token.ip.denied.todo: If you did not move that app, the token may have leaked: delete it and make a new one.
security.kind.token.ip.denied.what: A valid API token was used from an address it is not allowed from.

"Directly" is the usual choice for such an application.
mgmt.cloudflare.notes.guard: Cosmos will answer for this address only to connections from Cloudflare's network and from your local network. Whoever asks this server for it directly is refused, and the attempt is recorded.
mgmt.cloudflare.notes.limits: Limits of Cloudflare's proxy on the free plan: at most 100 MB per upload, an answer must begin within about two minutes, and long-lived connections (live updates, terminals) are cut from time to time.
mgmt.cloudflare.notes.bans: A firewall ban on this server (Fail2ban) cannot cut off a visitor who comes through Cloudflare: the connection is Cloudflare's. Cosmos' own SmartShield still goes by the visitor's real address.
mgmt.cloudflare.notes.ssl: At Cloudflare, the domain's SSL/TLS mode must be "Full (strict)" (SSL/TLS > Overview).
mgmt.cloudflare.switch.failed: The change could not be saved.
mgmt.cloudflare.switch.tipManaged: Cosmos sets this at Cloudflare for you. A change made by hand at Cloudflare is put back within ten minutes.
mgmt.cloudflare.switch.tipByHand: Cosmos does not manage this record: this only tells Cosmos how the record is set at Cloudflare, so that it believes and refuses the right visitors.
mgmt.cloudflare.confirm.title: Serve {{host}} through Cloudflare?
mgmt.cloudflare.confirm.byHand: Cosmos does not manage this record, so nothing is changed at Cloudflare: the proxy (orange cloud) must be on for it there.
mgmt.cloudflare.last.title: Nothing is served through Cloudflare any more
mgmt.cloudflare.last.text: Cosmos still believes Cloudflare's addresses when they say who the visitor is. With no address served through Cloudflare there is no reason to: stop believing them?
mgmt.cloudflare.ranges.refreshed: Cloudflare's current list is in use: {{count}} ranges.
mgmt.cloudflare.title: Cloudflare
mgmt.cloudflare.port.bad: Visitors reach Cosmos on port {{port}}, which Cloudflare does not pass on (it passes HTTPS on ports {{ports}}). Addresses can only be served directly until that changes.
mgmt.cloudflare.zone.noToken: No API token is stored for this domain: Cosmos cannot write its records. Connect it again.
mgmt.cloudflare.zone.byHand: Cosmos gets this domain's certificate through Cloudflare, but does not manage its records ("manage records" is off): you create each address at Cloudflare yourself.
mgmt.cloudflare.noHosts: No address under this domain yet. Give an application one with "Domains" on its card (ServApps).
mgmt.cloudflare.mixed: Some addresses are served directly: their records show this server's public address to anyone who looks them up. Cloudflare filters the traffic of the addresses that go through it; it does not hide the server.
mgmt.cloudflare.ranges.title: Cloudflare's addresses
mgmt.cloudflare.ranges.trusted: For an address served through Cloudflare, Cosmos takes the visitor's address from what Cloudflare reports, when the connection comes from one of Cloudflare's own addresses. For every other address, and from everyone else, such a report is ignored.
mgmt.cloudflare.ranges.untrusted: Nothing is served through Cloudflare: Cosmos takes every visitor's address from the connection itself.
mgmt.cloudflare.ranges.builtin: List in use: {{count}} ranges, the one built into Cosmos (Cloudflare's list of {{date}}).
mgmt.cloudflare.ranges.fetched: List in use: {{count}} ranges, fetched from Cloudflare on {{date}}.
mgmt.cloudflare.ranges.refreshTip: Asks api.cloudflare.com for its published address ranges and uses them if they are a list of public networks. While an address is served through Cloudflare, Cosmos also does this once a week.
mgmt.cloudflare.noAnswer: The server did not answer. Confirm your password again if it asks, then retry.
mgmt.cloudflare.work.takeover: Noting which records Cosmos may replace…
mgmt.cloudflare.panelFailed: The panel's address could not be set.
mgmt.cloudflare.work.shield: Telling Cosmos that the panel comes through Cloudflare…
mgmt.cloudflare.connect.title: Connect Cloudflare
mgmt.cloudflare.connect.intro: With an API token of your Cloudflare account, Cosmos gives each application an address under your domain, keeps those addresses pointed at this server when its public address changes, and gets real certificates without opening any other port. Records Cosmos did not create are never changed.
mgmt.cloudflare.connect.howToken: Create the token at Cloudflare: My Profile > API Tokens > Create Token > "Edit zone DNS". Permissions: Zone > DNS > Edit and Zone > Zone > Read. Zone Resources: Include > Specific zone > your domain. A token limited to that one domain is all Cosmos needs.
mgmt.cloudflare.connect.useStored: Or use the token already stored for:
mgmt.cloudflare.connect.tokenHelp: It is stored on this server with the domain, is never shown again and is sent to api.cloudflare.com only.
mgmt.cloudflare.connect.broad: This token sees {{count}} domains of your account. Cosmos only needs the one you connect: a token limited to it (Zone Resources > Specific zone) is safer, and you can replace this one later.
mgmt.cloudflare.connect.typeZone: The token sees more domains than are listed. Type yours:
mgmt.cloudflare.connect.reading: Reading the records of {{zone}} at Cloudflare…
mgmt.cloudflare.review.panelTitle: The address of the Cosmos panel
mgmt.cloudflare.review.panelInvalid: Expected {{zone}} itself or a name under it, such as cosmos.{{zone}}.
mgmt.cloudflare.review.source.keep: The panel keeps the address it has now.
mgmt.cloudflare.review.source.apex: Proposed because {{zone}} already goes through Cloudflare to this server: on port {{port}} it reaches Cosmos, without any new record.
mgmt.cloudflare.review.source.current: This is the panel's address today.
mgmt.cloudflare.review.source.default: Proposed: a name of its own for the panel. Cosmos creates its record.
mgmt.cloudflare.review.panelChange: What changes for you: the panel keeps answering at the address you use now ({{current}}) and you stay logged in there. At {{address}} you log in once more, because a login belongs to one address. That address works from outside once your router forwards port {{port}} to this server; until its certificate has arrived (a few minutes) the browser shows a warning there.
mgmt.cloudflare.review.panelShield: {{host}} goes through Cloudflare's proxy: tell Cosmos so. It then takes visitors' addresses from Cloudflare for this name, and refuses whoever asks this server for it directly (your local network always gets in).
mgmt.cloudflare.review.recordsTitle: What Cosmos will do at Cloudflare
mgmt.cloudflare.review.notManaged: "Manage records" is off: Cosmos writes no record. You create each address at Cloudflare yourself.
mgmt.cloudflare.review.noRows: Nothing yet: no application has an address under this domain. Each address you attach later gets its record then.
mgmt.cloudflare.review.newUnknown: A record to this server's public address
mgmt.cloudflare.review.alreadyHere: This name already has a proxied record that points at this server: Cosmos will not touch it.
mgmt.cloudflare.review.replace: Let Cosmos replace this record with one that points at this server
mgmt.cloudflare.review.untouchedTitle: Not touched: the {{count}} other records of {{zone}}
mgmt.cloudflare.review.truncated: This domain has more records than Cosmos reads (5000): the list above is not complete.
mgmt.cloudflare.review.caa: The domain has CAA records that do not name letsencrypt.org: Let's Encrypt will refuse to issue certificates for it until one is added at Cloudflare.
mgmt.cloudflare.review.wildcard: The domain already has a wildcard record (*): names without a record of their own resolve to wherever it points.
mgmt.cloudflare.review.privateAddress: The records would point at a local address ({{address}}): they work on your network only.
mgmt.cloudflare.review.addressLater: Cosmos does not know this server's public address yet: it looks it up when it writes the records.
mgmt.cloudflare.review.settingsTitle: How the domain is set up
mgmt.cloudflare.review.settings: Certificates from Let's Encrypt, proven through Cloudflare's DNS: nothing has to be reachable on port 80 or 443 of your address. One certificate for {{zone}} and every name under it. Cosmos creates a record for each address you attach to an application and removes it when you detach it; there is no catch-all (wildcard) record.
mgmt.cloudflare.options.wildcardCertific: One certificate for the domain and all names under it (recommended: a new address works at once, and the names do not appear in public certificate logs)
mgmt.cloudflare.options.manageRecords: Cosmos creates and updates the records of the addresses it serves (recommended). Off: you keep every record by hand.
mgmt.cloudflare.options.wildcardRecord: One catch-all record (*) instead of a record per address. Not recommended: every name under the domain then leads to this server, and no address can be switched to Cloudflare's proxy on its own.
mgmt.cloudflare.options.provided: A certificate you provide (for example a Cloudflare Origin CA certificate) is possible too, with "Add a domain by hand". Browsers only accept an Origin CA certificate through Cloudflare's proxy: an address served directly, or opened on your local network, would show a warning.
mgmt.cloudflare.options.manual: Add a domain by hand instead
mgmt.cloudflare.done.title: {{zone}} is connected.
mgmt.cloudflare.done.panel: The panel now also answers at {{address}}. Log in there once; the address you are using keeps working.
mgmt.cloudflare.done.through: Cosmos expects visitors of the panel's name through Cloudflare, and refuses that name to anyone else outside your local network.
mgmt.cloudflare.done.next: Next: on the card of an application (ServApps), "Domains" gives it an address under {{zone}}, and there you choose for each address whether it goes through Cloudflare or directly. The certificate arrives within a few minutes; the list above shows it.
mgmt.cloudflare.done.router: From outside, every address is opened with port {{port}}. Your router must forward that port to this server (Configuration > HTTP > Internet access can ask it to).
activity.cloudflare.shield: Change how the address is served
activity.cloudflare.takeover: Let Cosmos replace the existing record
mgmt.cloudflare.token.expired: This token has expired. Create a new one at Cloudflare (My Profile > API Tokens).
mgmt.cloudflare.token.disabled: This token is switched off at Cloudflare. Switch it on there (My Profile > API Tokens), or create a new one.
mgmt.cloudflare.token.invalid: Cloudflare does not know this token. Check that all of it was copied; a token is shown only once, when it is created.
mgmt.cloudflare.token.malformed: This is not an API token: one is a single line of letters, digits, "_" and "-", without spaces.
mgmt.cloudflare.token.globalKey: This is the Global API Key of your Cloudflare account: it can change everything in the account, and Cosmos does not accept it. Create an API token instead (My Profile > API Tokens > Create Token > "Edit zone DNS"), limited to this one domain.
mgmt.cloudflare.token.originCaKey: This is an Origin CA key, which only makes certificates. Cosmos needs an API token (My Profile > API Tokens > Create Token > "Edit zone DNS").
mgmt.cloudflare.token.oauth: This is a login of Cloudflare's command line tool, not an API token. Create one under My Profile > API Tokens.
mgmt.cloudflare.token.noZones: The token is valid but sees no domain. It needs two permissions for your domain: Zone > Zone > Read and Zone > DNS > Edit.
mgmt.cloudflare.token.unreachable: Cloudflare could not be reached from this server just now. Try again in a moment.
mgmt.cloudflare.token.rateLimited: Cloudflare asks to slow down: try again in a few minutes.
mgmt.cloudflare.failure.invalidToken: Cloudflare does not accept the token (wrong, expired or deleted). Paste a current one under Configuration > Domains.
mgmt.cloudflare.failure.malformedToken: What is stored is not an API token. Paste one under Configuration > Domains.
mgmt.cloudflare.failure.forbidden: The token may not do this. It needs Zone > Zone > Read and Zone > DNS > Edit for this domain.
mgmt.cloudflare.failure.notFound: The token does not see this domain at Cloudflare.
mgmt.cloudflare.failure.rateLimited: Cloudflare asks to slow down. Cosmos tries again by itself.
mgmt.cloudflare.failure.unreachable: Cloudflare could not be reached from this server. Cosmos tries again by itself.
mgmt.cloudflare.failure.server: Cloudflare has a problem of its own right now. Cosmos tries again by itself.
mgmt.cloudflare.cannot.notServed: Cosmos does not serve this address.
mgmt.cloudflare.cannot.notCloudflare: This address is not under a domain connected to Cloudflare.
mgmt.cloudflare.cannot.noToken: No API token is stored for this domain. Connect it again under Configuration > Domains.
mgmt.cloudflare.cannot.wildcardRecord: This domain publishes one wildcard record for all its names, so this address has no record of its own to switch. Turn "wildcard record" off for the domain under Configuration > Domains.
mgmt.cloudflare.cannot.httpOnly: This domain is served over plain HTTP. Choose a certificate for it under Configuration > Domains first.
mgmt.cloudflare.cannot.ownPort: A URL answers for this name on a port of its own, which Cloudflare does not pass on. A name is either through Cloudflare for all its ports or for none.
mgmt.cloudflare.cannot.port: Cloudflare passes HTTPS on only on ports {{ports}}, and Cosmos is published on port {{port}}.
mgmt.cloudflare.cannot.privateAddress: The records of this server point at a local address, which Cloudflare cannot reach.
mgmt.cloudflare.cannot.other: This address cannot be served through Cloudflare.
mgmt.cloudflare.mismatch.expectsProxy: At Cloudflare this record is not proxied, but Cosmos is told it is: visitors reach this server directly and are refused. Switch the proxy on at Cloudflare (orange cloud), or choose "directly" here.
mgmt.cloudflare.mismatch.expectsDirect: At Cloudflare this record is proxied, but Cosmos is told it is not: Cosmos sees Cloudflare's addresses instead of the visitors'. Choose "through Cloudflare" here.
mgmt.cloudflare.preview.update: will get this server's current address
mgmt.cloudflare.preview.remove: Cosmos' own record, no longer used: will be removed
mgmt.cloudflare.record.pending: The record is being written at Cloudflare: this takes up to a minute.
mgmt.cloudflare.record.apexNone: This is the domain's own name. Cosmos never writes its record: create it at Cloudflare yourself.
mgmt.cloudflare.record.apexHereProxied: The domain's own record exists at Cloudflare, goes through its proxy and points at this server. Cosmos does not touch it.
mgmt.cloudflare.record.apexHereDnsOnly: The domain's own record exists at Cloudflare and points straight at this server, without the proxy. Cosmos does not touch it.
mgmt.cloudflare.record.apexElsewhereProx: The domain's own record exists at Cloudflare and goes through its proxy. Cosmos does not touch it, and cannot tell from here whether it leads to this server.
mgmt.cloudflare.record.apexElsewhereDnsO: The domain's own record exists at Cloudflare and points at another address than this server's. Cosmos does not touch it.
mgmt.cloudflare.record.foreignProxied: A record for this name already exists at Cloudflare, through its proxy, and Cosmos did not create it: it is left as it is.
mgmt.cloudflare.record.foreignDnsOnly: A record for this name already exists at Cloudflare, without the proxy, and Cosmos did not create it: it is left as it is.
mgmt.cloudflare.record.byHand: Cosmos does not manage the records of this domain: the record is yours to create at Cloudflare.
mgmt.cloudflare.record.proxied: The record exists at Cloudflare and goes through its proxy.
mgmt.cloudflare.record.direct: The record exists at Cloudflare and points straight at this server.
mgmt.cloudflare.ssl.strict: Cloudflare's SSL/TLS mode for this domain is "Full (strict)": it checks this server's certificate.
mgmt.cloudflare.ssl.full: Cloudflare's SSL/TLS mode for this domain is "Full": the connection to this server is encrypted, but Cloudflare does not check the certificate. Set it to "Full (strict)" at Cloudflare (SSL/TLS > Overview).
mgmt.cloudflare.ssl.flexible: Cloudflare's SSL/TLS mode for this domain is "Flexible", which does not check this server's certificate. Set it to "Full (strict)" at Cloudflare (SSL/TLS > Overview).
mgmt.cloudflare.ssl.off: Cloudflare's SSL/TLS mode for this domain is "Off": nothing reaches this server over HTTPS through Cloudflare. Set it to "Full (strict)" at Cloudflare (SSL/TLS > Overview).
mgmt.cloudflare.ssl.unknown: For addresses served through Cloudflare, its SSL/TLS mode for the domain must be "Full (strict)" (at Cloudflare: SSL/TLS > Overview). This token may not read that setting, so Cosmos cannot check it.
mgmt.cloudflare.zone.readOnly: The token may read the records of this domain but not change them. Add the permission Zone > DNS > Edit.
mgmt.cloudflare.zone.noDns: The token sees this domain but not its records. Add the permission Zone > DNS > Edit.
mgmt.cloudflare.zone.canEdit: The token may change the records of this domain. Nothing was created or changed to find out.
mgmt.cloudflare.zone.unknown: Cosmos could not tell whether the token may change the records of this domain. The first record it writes will show.
mgmt.reach.check.record.pending: The record is being written at Cloudflare: this takes up to a minute.
mgmt.reach.check.record.foreign: A record for this name exists at Cloudflare that Cosmos did not create: Cosmos leaves it as it is.
mgmt.reach.check.record.errorInvalidToke: Cloudflare does not accept the stored API token (wrong, expired or deleted): the record cannot be written. Paste a current token.
mgmt.reach.check.record.errorMalformedTo: What is stored for this domain is not an API token: the record cannot be written.
mgmt.reach.check.record.errorForbidden: The API token may not change this domain's records at Cloudflare. It needs Zone > Zone > Read and Zone > DNS > Edit.
mgmt.reach.check.record.errorNotFound: The API token does not see this domain at Cloudflare: the record cannot be written.
mgmt.reach.check.record.errorRateLimited: Cloudflare asked Cosmos to slow down: the record is written a little later.
mgmt.reach.check.record.errorUnreachable: Cloudflare could not be reached from this server: the record is written once it can.
mgmt.reach.check.record.errorOther: The record could not be written at Cloudflare. Configuration > Domains shows the reason.
mgmt.reach.check.dns.throughShield: The name leads to Cloudflare, which passes visitors on to this server.
mgmt.reach.check.dns.shieldNotYet: The name still points straight at this server although it is set to go through Cloudflare: the change is on its way, or the proxy was switched off at Cloudflare. Visitors who get this answer are refused.
mgmt.reach.check.dns.behindCloudflare: The name leads to Cloudflare's proxy, but here it is set to be served directly: Cosmos then takes Cloudflare's addresses for the visitors. Set it to "through Cloudflare" under Domains.
mgmt.reach.check.shield.on: Served through Cloudflare: Cosmos answers for this name to Cloudflare's network and to your local network only.
mgmt.reach.check.shield.port: Set to go through Cloudflare, but visitors use port {{port}}, which Cloudflare does not pass on (it passes HTTPS on 443, 2053, 2083, 2087, 2096 and 8443).
mgmt.cloudflare.review.apexCookie: Good to know before choosing the domain itself: a browser sends a login to every port of a name. Whatever answers https://{{zone}} without a port (another machine, if your router sends that port elsewhere) receives the panel's login cookie with each visit, and so does every name under {{zone}}. If those are not all yours alone, give the panel a name of its own instead ({{own}}).
mgmt.cloudflare.ranges.limit: What this does and does not do: it keeps out everyone who does not come through Cloudflare's network. That network is shared by all of Cloudflare's customers, so it is not proof that a request passed your own Cloudflare settings. Logins, two-factor codes and SmartShield apply to every request as before.
mgmt.cloudflare.pulls.noAnswer: Cosmos did not answer. If you reach this page through Cloudflare, wait a moment and reload it.
mgmt.cloudflare.pulls.upload.done: Cloudflare has the certificate for {{zone}} and "Zone-level" is switched on there. Cosmos no longer holds the key. Start the test below.
mgmt.cloudflare.pulls.upload.notEnabled: Cloudflare has the certificate for {{zone}}, but Cosmos could not switch "Zone-level" on there: do that at Cloudflare (SSL/TLS > Origin Server > Authenticated Origin Pulls). Cosmos no longer holds the key.
mgmt.cloudflare.pulls.title: Proof that a request came through Cloudflare
mgmt.cloudflare.pulls.intro: Cloudflare's addresses are shared by all its customers, so a request from one of them has not necessarily passed your domain there. Cloudflare's proxy can present a certificate to this server with every connection (Cloudflare calls this "Authenticated Origin Pulls"), and Cosmos can require it for the addresses served through Cloudflare. Your local network never needs it: the panel stays reachable at home whatever is set here.
mgmt.cloudflare.pulls.kind.label: Which certificate Cloudflare presents
mgmt.cloudflare.pulls.kind.help: Choose one to see what it proves and what to do at Cloudflare.
mgmt.cloudflare.pulls.shared.built: Cloudflare's certificate as built into this version of Cosmos: valid until {{date}}, SHA-256 fingerprint {{fingerprint}}. It is never fetched from the internet: you can compare it with the one Cloudflare publishes.
mgmt.cloudflare.pulls.handover.text: Cloudflare needs this certificate and its private key to present it. Cosmos can upload both, or show them to you once. After either, Cosmos no longer has the key.
mgmt.cloudflare.pulls.handover.tokenHelp: A Cloudflare API token with the permission Zone > SSL and Certificates > Edit for {{zone}}. Used for this upload, not kept. You can delete it at Cloudflare afterwards.
mgmt.cloudflare.pulls.steps.titleOwn: At Cloudflare, when you upload the certificate yourself:
mgmt.cloudflare.pulls.anyway.title: Enforce although some requests have no certificate?
mgmt.cloudflare.pulls.anyway.text: From now on such requests are refused. Requests with the certificate, and everything from your local network, are answered as before. If this browser is cut off, Cosmos goes back to testing by itself after three minutes.
mgmt.cloudflare.pulls.reveal.title: The certificate and its private key
mgmt.cloudflare.pulls.reveal.once: This is shown once: Cosmos no longer has the key. Whoever has it can pass as Cloudflare for your domain, so paste it at Cloudflare and keep it nowhere else. If it gets lost before it is uploaded, make a new certificate.
mgmt.cloudflare.pulls.kind.ownText: Cosmos makes a certificate and you give it to Cloudflare for your domain. Only your domain at Cloudflare can present it, so it proves that a request passed your own Cloudflare settings. Free on every Cloudflare plan. It is valid for a year; Cosmos reminds you before it ends.
mgmt.cloudflare.pulls.kind.sharedText: One switch at Cloudflare, nothing to upload. It proves that Cloudflare's proxy made the connection for some domain that has this switched on, and any Cloudflare customer can switch it on for a domain of theirs. It does not prove that a request passed your domain.
mgmt.cloudflare.pulls.refusal.noKind: Choose which certificate Cloudflare presents first.
mgmt.cloudflare.pulls.refusal.noCertific: Make a certificate and give it to Cloudflare first.
mgmt.cloudflare.pulls.refusal.sharedExpi: Cloudflare's certificate built into this version of Cosmos has expired. Update Cosmos, or use a certificate of your own.
mgmt.cloudflare.pulls.refusal.nothingVer: No request has verified yet, so enforcing would refuse everything that comes through Cloudflare. Open an address from outside your network and wait until it is counted.
mgmt.cloudflare.pulls.refusal.failing: Requests without the certificate arrived within the last minute.
mgmt.cloudflare.pulls.refusal.enforcing: Stop enforcing first: this change would stop requests from verifying.
mgmt.cloudflare.pulls.refusal.noPending: Cosmos no longer holds the key of this certificate: it is kept for 15 minutes and handed over once. Make a new certificate.
mgmt.cloudflare.pulls.refusal.twoCertifi: Two certificates are accepted already. Stop accepting the one Cloudflare no longer uses first.
mgmt.cloudflare.pulls.refusal.notCloudfl: This is not a domain connected to Cloudflare.
mgmt.cloudflare.pulls.refusal.lastCertif: This is the only certificate: without it nothing would verify. Switch the check off first, or make a new certificate.
mgmt.cloudflare.pulls.refusal.notSeen: No request has verified with the other certificate yet. Upload it at Cloudflare and wait until Cloudflare uses it.
mgmt.cloudflare.pulls.refusal.other: This is not possible right now.
mgmt.cloudflare.pulls.upload.forbidden: The token Cosmos has stored may not upload certificates: it only edits DNS records, and Cosmos does not ask for more. Either paste a token made for this one step (at Cloudflare: My Profile > API Tokens > Create Token > Custom token, permission Zone > SSL and Certificates > Edit, for this domain only); Cosmos uses it once and does not keep it. Or show the certificate and its key and upload them at Cloudflare yourself.
mgmt.cloudflare.pulls.upload.invalidToke: Cloudflare does not accept this token (wrong, expired or deleted).
mgmt.cloudflare.pulls.upload.malformedTo: This is not an API token: one is a single line of letters, digits, "_" and "-".
mgmt.cloudflare.pulls.upload.notFound: Neither token sees this domain at Cloudflare.
mgmt.cloudflare.pulls.upload.rateLimited: Cloudflare asks to slow down: try again in a few minutes.
mgmt.cloudflare.pulls.upload.unreachable: Cloudflare could not be reached from this server just now. Try again in a moment.
mgmt.cloudflare.pulls.upload.server: Cloudflare has a problem of its own right now. Try again in a moment.
mgmt.cloudflare.pulls.problem.wrongCerti: another certificate than the expected one
mgmt.cloudflare.pulls.steps.open: At Cloudflare, open your domain, then SSL/TLS > Origin Server, and there the tab "Authenticated Origin Pulls".
mgmt.cloudflare.pulls.steps.upload: Under "Zone-level", choose "Upload certificate" and paste the certificate and the private key Cosmos shows you.
mgmt.cloudflare.pulls.steps.strict: SSL/TLS > Overview must say "Full (strict)": with "Flexible" or "Off" Cloudflare presents no certificate.
mgmt.cloudflare.pulls.steps.wait: Come back here and start the test. A change at Cloudflare takes up to a minute to be in use.
mgmt.cloudflare.pulls.state.off: Off: a request for an address served through Cloudflare is accepted from any of Cloudflare's addresses.
mgmt.cloudflare.pulls.state.test: Testing: Cosmos asks Cloudflare's proxy for its certificate and counts what it gets. Nothing is refused yet.
mgmt.cloudflare.pulls.state.unconfirmed: Enforcing, not confirmed yet. If this browser cannot reach Cosmos any more, Cosmos goes back to testing by itself in {{seconds}} seconds.
mgmt.cloudflare.pulls.state.enforce: Enforcing: a request for an address served through Cloudflare is answered only when Cloudflare's proxy presented the certificate, or when it comes from your local network.
mgmt.cloudflare.pulls.expiry.sharedSoon: Cloudflare's certificate built into this version of Cosmos ends in {{days}} days ({{date}}). Cloudflare will present a new one by then: update Cosmos before that date, or change to a certificate of your own.
mgmt.cloudflare.pulls.expiry.sharedOver: Cloudflare's certificate built into this version of Cosmos has ended ({{date}}): nothing verifies with it any more. Update Cosmos, or change to a certificate of your own.
mgmt.cloudflare.pulls.expiry.ownSoon: Your certificate ends in {{days}} days ({{date}}). Make a new one below and give it to Cloudflare before then; both are accepted during the change.
mgmt.cloudflare.pulls.expiry.ownOver: Your certificate has ended ({{date}}): nothing verifies with it any more. Make a new one below and give it to Cloudflare.
mgmt.cloudflare.pulls.cert.waiting: Made just now, not given to Cloudflare yet. Cosmos holds its key for {{minutes}} more minutes.
mgmt.cloudflare.pulls.cert.unused: Made, never given to Cloudflare, and its key is gone: nobody can present it.
mgmt.cloudflare.pulls.cert.verified: In use: Cloudflare presented it at {{time}}.
mgmt.cloudflare.pulls.cert.handed: Given to Cloudflare. No request has presented it since counting began.
mgmt.cloudflare.pulls.verdict.none: No request has come through Cloudflare since counting began. Open one of these addresses from outside your network (a phone on mobile data, Wi-Fi off): {{hosts}}
mgmt.cloudflare.pulls.verdict.clean: {{verified}} requests came through Cloudflare, each with a certificate that verified. Enforcing will not refuse them.
mgmt.cloudflare.pulls.verdict.nothing: {{failed}} requests came from Cloudflare's addresses and none presented the certificate ({{reasons}}). At Cloudflare it is not in place or not switched on yet: go through the steps above, then wait a minute.
mgmt.cloudflare.pulls.verdict.settled: {{verified}} requests verified; {{failed}} earlier ones did not ({{reasons}}), none within the last minute. Those came while the setting was still spreading at Cloudflare.
mgmt.cloudflare.pulls.verdict.failing: {{verified}} requests verified, {{failed}} did not ({{reasons}}), some of them within the last minute, for: {{hosts}}. If you changed something at Cloudflare just now, wait a minute. If not, these are requests that did not pass your domain at Cloudflare: exactly what enforcing refuses.
mgmt.cloudflare.pulls.verdict.enforcing: Since enforcing began: {{verified}} requests answered, {{failed}} refused.
mgmt.cloudflare.pulls.verdict.enforcingR: Since enforcing began: {{verified}} requests answered, {{failed}} refused ({{reasons}}). If your own visits through Cloudflare stopped working, press "Stop enforcing".
header.notification.message.originPullEx: The certificate Cloudflare's proxy presents to this server expires in {{Vars}}. After that, requests through Cloudflare are refused while the check is enforced. See Configuration > Domains > Cloudflare, "Proof that a request came through Cloudflare".
header.notification.message.originPullSt: Requiring a certificate from Cloudflare's proxy was switched on but not confirmed within three minutes, so Cosmos went back to testing: nothing is refused. If the panel stopped answering through Cloudflare at that moment, the certificate is not in place at Cloudflare yet. See Configuration > Domains > Cloudflare.
fail2ban.through.cloudflare: Addresses served through Cloudflare: {{n}}. A ban works for whoever connects to this server directly. Visitors who come through Cloudflare never reach the firewall, only Cloudflare does: Cosmos does not report them to Fail2ban, so nothing they do leads to a ban here, and nobody can get somebody else's address banned by claiming it. SmartShield still blocks them inside Cosmos, by the address Cloudflare reports. To stop them earlier, block them at Cloudflare.
fail2ban.through.proxy: Reverse proxies Cosmos trusts (Configuration, HTTP): {{n}}. Visitors who come through them never reach the firewall either and are not reported to Fail2ban. Whoever connects to this server directly is banned as usual.
fail2ban.cloudflare.kept: Also never banned: Cloudflare's {{count}} address ranges. Every visitor of an address served through Cloudflare arrives from them, so a ban of one would cut them all off. Cosmos keeps them on the list by itself, replaces them when Cloudflare's list changes and takes them off when nothing is served through Cloudflare any more.
fail2ban.cloudflare.missing: Cloudflare's address ranges belong on this list while an address is served through Cloudflare, and the jails run with {{ignored}} of {{count}} of them. Cosmos adds them by itself within a minute. If this stays, save the settings below once.
fail2ban.self.forwarded: You reach this page through Cloudflare or a reverse proxy, which reports your address as {{ip}}. A ban at the firewall cannot cut this connection off, whatever address it names.

security.kind.access.foreign.denied.what: A request to the panel was refused because it did not come from the panel's own pages: another website, another application of the same domain, or an address opened by hand.
security.kind.access.foreign.denied.todo: Nothing to do if it happened once: opening an address of the panel's API in the address bar does this too. If it repeats while you are logged in, a page you have open elsewhere is trying to act with your login: close it, and look at which address it came from.

mgmt.localNames.note.intro: A .local address is not looked up in DNS: the device asks the local network (mDNS), and Cosmos, through Avahi, answers with the server's address. So it works on the home network only, and only on devices that ask the network:
mgmt.localNames.note.ip: The server's address, {{ip}}: https://{{ip}}:{{port}} opens the panel, and an app can have an address of its own made of the server's address and a port (the last proposal of its URL form).
mgmt.localNames.note.ipNoPort: The server's address, {{ip}}: an app can have an address of its own made of the server's address and a port (the last proposal of its URL form).
mgmt.localNames.note.domain: Its internet address, when a domain is attached to the app (Configuration > Domains): it works everywhere and has a certificate every device trusts.
mgmt.localNames.note.router: A DNS entry on your router or Pi-hole that points a name at {{ip}}: every device on the network then resolves it. Pick a name that does not end in .local (for example app.home.arpa) and add it to the app's URL as well: devices send .local names to mDNS only.
mgmt.localNames.note.certificate: The browser warns about the certificate the first time: no public authority certifies a .local name, so Cosmos signs these addresses with its own authority. Every .local address of an app is on that certificate. Install the authority once on each device and the warning is gone for good:
mgmt.localNames.note.certificateApps: . Apps on Android, smart TVs and many apps on phones ignore an authority added by hand; use the internet address there.

mgmt.localNames.problem.notFound: {{name}}: there is no such interface on the server.
mgmt.localNames.problem.noIPv4: {{name}}: the interface has no IPv4 address.
mgmt.localNames.interfaces: Network interfaces to publish on (empty: the ones facing the local network, chosen automatically)
mgmt.localNames.interfacesHelp: Names as the server spells them, separated by commas (for example eno1, wlan0). Docker's networks, VPNs and Tailscale are never chosen automatically.
mgmt.localNames.off: Cosmos does not publish .local names (Configuration > HTTP, "Publish .local domains"): such a name only works where a DNS entry points it at the server.
mgmt.localNames.absent: Avahi is not running on the server, so no device can resolve .local names. Install and start it (Debian, Ubuntu: apt install avahi-daemon).
mgmt.localNames.noInterface: No network interface facing the local network was found, so the names are not published. Name the interface in Configuration > HTTP.
mgmt.localNames.multiLabel: A name with a dot before .local is not resolved by Windows nor by most Linux machines: prefer a single word, such as app.local.
mgmt.localNames.foreign: Another device ({{from}}) also answers for this name.
mgmt.localNames.notYet: Published on {{where}} once the address is saved.
mgmt.localNames.answered: Published on {{where}}, and answered on the network.
mgmt.localNames.unanswered: Published on {{where}}, but no answer came back on the network just now: check again in a moment.
mgmt.localNames.registering: Being published: Avahi first checks that no other device uses the name.
mgmt.localNames.hostName: The server's own name: Avahi answers it.
mgmt.localNames.conflictFrom: Another device ({{from}}) already uses this name, so Cosmos does not publish it. Give the app another address, or rename the other device; Cosmos tries again every ten minutes and on every save.
mgmt.localNames.conflict: Another device or program already uses this name, so Cosmos does not publish it. Give the app another address, or rename the other device; Cosmos tries again every ten minutes and on every save.
mgmt.localNames.tooMany: Not published: Cosmos publishes at most 256 .local names.
mgmt.localNames.summaryBad: {{count}} of the {{total}} .local names are not published: {{names}}.
mgmt.localNames.summaryUnanswered: Published on {{where}}; no answer came back just now for {{names}}.
mgmt.localNames.summaryNone: Ready: .local names will be published on {{where}}.
mgmt.localNames.summaryOk: {{count}} .local names published on {{where}} and answered on the network.
mgmt.localNames.avahiAllow: Avahi announces the server's own name on every interface, Docker's included, so the server and its containers may find it at a Docker address. Cosmos publishes the app names on {{names}} only, whatever Avahi does. To make Avahi do the same, set allow-interfaces={{names}} in the [server] section of /etc/avahi/avahi-daemon.conf and restart Avahi.
mgmt.localNames.device.windows: Windows 10 and 11: yes, without Bonjour, as long as the network is set to "Private" (on a "Public" network Windows may block the answers).
mgmt.localNames.device.android: Android 12 and newer: usually (Android resolves .local names since late 2021). Some Chrome versions fail on some names where Firefox works; never over a VPN or mobile data.
mgmt.localNames.device.linux: Linux: yes with Avahi and nss-mdns (most desktop distributions). Not with systemd-resolved alone, whose mDNS is off unless switched on.
mgmt.localNames.device.old: Android 11 and older, most smart TVs, consoles and many apps: no.
mgmt.localNames.device.remote: Away from home (Tailscale, VPN, mobile data): no, the names stay on the local network.
